text: Lesson 19 loaded orders.csv the quick way. This lesson is about loading it properly, from three different real-world sources, with options that actually matter once you start doing anything with the data beyond printing it.

parse_dates tells pandas to convert order_date into a real datetime64 column while it reads the file. That one argument is the difference between order_date being a pretty string and being something you can actually do date math with.

Here's why that conversion matters: filtering for orders on or after January 10th only works reliably because order_date is now a true datetime type. Twelve of the twenty orders match — order 1009 through order 1020.

pd.read_json reads the orders.json file Lesson 15 wrote right back into a DataFrame. Interesting detail: that JSON stored quantity as a quoted string, but read_json is smart enough to infer it should be a real int64 column anyway.

This course's data lives in a CSV, not an Excel file, but the syntax is worth knowing — stakeholders export Excel workbooks all the time. read_excel needs the openpyxl package installed, and sheet_name picks which sheet to load.

However you load a DataFrame, selecting and filtering it works the same way. Next lesson: picking exact columns and rows out of orders.csv, including the two real problem rows you already know are in there.
